Journeyings
jẽr´nĭ-ĭngz
n. pl. (the successive stages of a march; travels — rendering Hebrew massa and Greek hodoiporia)
From journey, Old French journee, a day's travel. The Hebrew massa means literally a pulling up of tent stakes — a departure by stages.

Biblical Definition

Journeyings is the Authorized Version's word for a life or a nation lived in stages. Of Israel: “Thus were the journeyings of the children of Israel according to their armies, when they set forward” (Num 10:28), and Moses was commanded to write them down: “And Moses wrote their goings out according to their journeys by the commandment of the LORD” (Num 33:2). The Hebrew word means the pulling up of tent pegs. A journeying is not a distance covered but a camp struck — the settled place abandoned at the command of God because the cloud moved. Paul uses the Greek equivalent in his catalogue of sufferings: “In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren” (2Co 11:26). The apostolic ministry was itinerant and dangerous, and the perils are listed by terrain and by company — including, last and worst, false brethren. Hebrews gathers the whole doctrine: the patriarchs “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13), which is the settled self-understanding of the people of God. They died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines journey as travel by land; a passage from one place to another; and journeyings as the successive stages or removals of a people on the march.

expand to see more

JOUR'NEY, n. The travel of a day; hence, travel by land to any distance and for any time.

2. Passage from one place to another; as, a long journey.

JOUR'NEYING, ppr. Traveling; passing from place to place.

JOUR'NEYINGS, n. plural. The successive removals or stages of a people on the march, as those of Israel in the wilderness.

Key Scripture

Numbers 10:28 — "Thus were the journeyings of the children of Israel according to their armies, when they set forward."

2 Corinthians 11:26 — "In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren;"

Hebrews 11:13 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

Numbers 33:2 — "And Moses wrote their goings out according to their journeys by the commandment of the LORD: and these are their journeys according to their goings out."

Modern Corruption

The pilgrim character of the Christian life is exchanged for permanence here, and the word journey is annexed to a private spirituality with no destination and no command.

expand to see more

Numbers 33 is a chapter of stage-names, written down at God's command, and it exists to teach a settled people that they were once a marching one. Hebrews 11:13 says the patriarchs confessed themselves strangers and pilgrims on the earth — a confession, publicly made, not a mood. Where the church forgets it, the marks are obvious: possessions held tightly, roots put down as though the camp were the country, and a Christianity indistinguishable in its ambitions from the world it passes through. The tent pegs come up at the command of God, and a man who has driven his in too deep will resent the cloud when it moves.

The modern religious use of journey runs the opposite way and empties the word from the other end. A journey with no destination, no map and no commander is not a pilgrimage but a wandering, and Scripture has a word for that too — the forty years were a judgment, not a spirituality. Israel's journeyings were by the commandment of the LORD, recorded stage by stage, toward a land already promised. Paul's were toward cities where Christ was not named. Both had a road and an end. Nothing in the Christian life is a journey merely for the travelling.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew massa (H4550), a pulling up of stakes, a setting forward by stages — Numbers 10:28, 33:2; Greek hodoiporia (G3597), a journeying, travel — 2 Corinthians 11:26, John 4:6.

expand to see more

Hebrew massa (H4550) — a departure by striking the tents; Numbers 10:28 and throughout Numbers 33.

Hebrew nasa (H5265) — to pull up stakes, journey; the verb behind the noun, used of every stage of the wilderness march.

Greek hodoiporia (G3597) — a journeying, travel; 2 Corinthians 11:26 and John 4:6 of the Lord wearied with His journey.

Greek parepidemos (G3927) — a sojourner, pilgrim; Hebrews 11:13, 1 Peter 1:1 and 2:11.

The Hebrew image is the tent peg: a journeying begins with leaving a place one had made comfortable.

Usage

"“Moses wrote their goings out… by the commandment of the LORD” — the stages were recorded on purpose."

"“In journeyings often… in perils among false brethren” — the last peril is the worst."

"“Strangers and pilgrims on the earth” — a confession, not a mood."
